lessons.title: Common Mistakes First-Time Property Investors Make

children.text: In 2019, Aakash, a 29-year-old software engineer in Noida, booked a ₹50 lakh under-construction flat in Greater Noida West. The broker promised possession in 2022 and prices rising 7% a year. Aakash chose a 20:80 subvention plan, paid ₹5 lakh of the price in cash "to save stamp duty," skipped a lawyer because the project was "bank approved," and put almost all his savings into it. The flat was delivered in 2025, three years late. In 2026 it is worth about ₹62 lakh. Aakash did not make one big mistake. He made several small ones that compounded. This final lesson brings the whole course together through the ten most common mistakes, so you can avoid every one of them.

body.text: Most property losses in India do not come from bad luck. They come from predictable mistakes: ignoring costs, trusting stories over numbers, borrowing too much, skipping checks and putting too many eggs in one illiquid basket.

body.title: Aakash's flat in 2026: promised vs actual value (₹ lakh, illustrative)
What did Aakash actually earn?
body.prompt: Aakash's flat went from ₹50 lakh in 2019 to about ₹62 lakh in 2026, over 7 years. What annual price growth (CAGR) does that represent, in %? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (62 ÷ 50)^(1/7) minus 1 ≈ 3.1% a year, below inflation for much of the period. And that is before counting stamp duty, three years of extra rent, interest on the loan, and the ₹5 lakh cash component that does not appear in his cost.

children.text: The Ten Mistakes
Mistake 1: Treating the price as the cost

The agreement price is only the start. Stamp duty, registration, brokerage, GST on under-construction flats, loan fees and move-in costs add roughly 8% to 12%, mostly in cash that banks will not lend. Budget for the full amount before you shortlist a single flat.

body.title: The real price of a Noida flat
body.prompt: A resale flat in Noida costs ₹85 lakh. Stamp duty is 7%, registration is 1%, and brokerage is 1% plus 18% GST. What do these three costs add up to, as a percentage of the price? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Stamp duty: ₹5.95 lakh. Registration: ₹85,000. Brokerage with GST: ₹1,00,300. Total: ₹7,80,300, or 9.18% of ₹85 lakh, before loan fees, repairs and shifting.

children.text: Mistake 2: Comparing gross yield with loan rates and FDs

A broker's "4% rental yield" is gross. After vacancy, maintenance, property tax, repairs and income tax, many flats net under 2%. Compare net yield with an FD's post-tax return and with the 7% to 9% your home loan costs.
Mistake 3: Believing "it doubled" stories

"My flat doubled in 12 years" is about 6% a year, before costs. Every property story should be converted into an annual rate, checked for its start date, and compared with the Nifty 50 TRI, gold or an FD over the same period.

body.caption: Doubling in 12 years: 2^(1/12) minus 1 ≈ 5.9% a year.

children.text: Mistake 4: Borrowing to the limit

The maximum loan a bank will sanction is not the loan you can safely carry. Leverage helps only when net yield plus appreciation beats the loan rate, and a 1 percentage point rate rise can add years and lakhs of interest. Keep EMIs comfortably within your income and hold an emergency fund.
Mistake 5: Skipping independent legal checks

"Bank approved" protects the bank, not you. Title, encumbrances and approvals need your own lawyer, original documents, an encumbrance certificate, a CERSAI search and a check that the building matches its sanctioned plan. It costs a tiny fraction of the property's price.
Mistake 6: Agreeing to a cash component

The small stamp duty saving comes with a smaller loan, a lower recorded cost that raises future capital gains tax, no legal proof of what you paid, and exposure to penalties that can equal the cash amount. Register at the real price and pay through the bank.
Mistake 7: Chasing under-construction discounts from weak developers

The discount on an under-construction flat pays you for GST, rent while waiting and delivery risk. A two-year delay can wipe it out. Check the developer's delivery record and RERA history, insist on a construction-linked plan, and treat subvention or "no EMI till possession" offers with deep suspicion.
Mistake 8: Ignoring liquidity and concentration

A flat can take months to sell and cannot be sold in parts. Putting most of your savings into one property, often in the same city as your job, leaves you exposed when you need cash. Keep liquid savings outside property and track real estate as a share of net worth.
Mistake 9: Letting urgency, emotion or tax drive the decision

"Last few units," "prices rise next week" and "everyone in the family has bought" are sales tactics, not analysis. Buying a flat you do not need just to save capital gains tax, or because relatives say rent is dead money, is equally risky. Decide on the investment first; optimise tax second.
Mistake 10: Assuming a flat is the only way to own real estate

Listed REITs, SM REIT schemes, realty funds, developer stocks and AIFs all offer real estate exposure with different trade-offs in ticket size, liquidity, income and risk. For many investors, especially those who already own a home, these routes add real estate far more efficiently than another flat.

body.title: Spot the biggest red flag
body.question: Which feature of a property pitch should worry a first-time buyer most?
options: The project is registered on the state RERA website
The developer offers a construction-linked payment plan
The seller asks for 20% of the price in cash and says the project is "bank approved, so no lawyer needed"
The flat's carpet area is stated in the agreement
body.explanation: A cash component and discouraging legal checks are two major red flags together. RERA registration, construction-linked plans and stated carpet areas are all signs of a properly structured deal.

body.title: The leverage test
body.question: A flat is expected to earn a 2.5% net yield and appreciate 4% a year. The home loan costs 8.5%. What does this suggest about borrowing heavily to buy it purely as an investment?
options: Borrowing will boost returns because property always rises
Borrowing will likely reduce returns, because 6.5% total return is below the 8.5% loan rate
The loan rate does not matter for investment returns
Borrowing is always better than paying cash
body.explanation: Leverage helps only when net yield plus appreciation exceeds the loan rate. At about 6.5% against 8.5%, each borrowed rupee costs more than it earns, dragging returns down and magnifying losses.

body.title: The most important document test
body.textWithBlank: Before paying any advance, a buyer should inspect the ___ title deeds, not photocopies.
body.explanation: Missing originals often mean the deeds are deposited with a lender or held in a dispute, problems photocopies and even an encumbrance certificate can miss.

body.text: Notice that almost none of these mistakes require expert knowledge to avoid. They require patience: to run the numbers, to read the documents, to say no to urgency and to consider alternatives. The discipline of a careful investor is the biggest edge you have in Indian real estate.

body.title: Capstone: the WhatsApp property pitch
body.scenario: Sneha, 33, a marketing manager in Hyderabad with ₹20 lakh in savings and a ₹1.5 lakh monthly salary, receives this message from a channel partner: "Pre-launch offer! 2BHK in Kollur, only ₹75 lakh (launch price ₹90 lakh). Pay 10% now, bank pays 70%, builder pays your EMI till possession in 2029. Registration at ₹65 lakh to save stamp duty, balance in cash. Airport-linked corridor, prices will double in 5 years. RERA number coming soon. Only 4 units left at this price, decide today."
body.prompt: Using everything you have learned in this course, identify every red flag in this pitch and explain what Sneha should do instead.
body.modelAnswer:
1. No RERA registration: "RERA number coming soon" means the project cannot legally be marketed or sold yet. This alone is a reason to walk away (Chapter 4).
2. Pre-launch booking: paying before registration, approvals and a registered agreement exposes her to the highest possible delivery and legal risk (Chapters 2 and 4).
3. Subvention structure: "builder pays your EMI till possession" leaves Sneha liable to the bank if the builder stops paying, and such schemes have been under CBI investigation (Chapter 2).
4. Cash component: registering at ₹65 lakh with ₹10 lakh in cash is illegal, reduces her loan eligibility and recorded cost, and exposes both parties to penalties (Chapter 4).
5. Unrealistic returns: "prices will double in 5 years" implies about 15% a year, far above typical long-run price growth (Chapters 1 and 3).
6. Fake anchor price: a "launch price" of ₹90 lakh for a project that has not launched is a marketing number, not a market value.
7. Urgency: "4 units left, decide today" is a pressure tactic (Chapter 6).
8. Affordability and concentration: ₹20 lakh savings would be consumed by the down payment and costs, leaving no emergency fund, with most of her wealth in one pre-launch flat (Chapters 3 and 6).
9. What she should do instead: decline this offer; if she wants to own a home, wait for RERA-registered projects from developers with strong delivery records, budget the full cost, register at the actual price, use a construction-linked plan and hire her own lawyer. If her goal is investment rather than a home, consider REITs and diversified funds, and run a buy vs rent comparison first.

body.title: The Complete Pre-Purchase Checklist
steps: Decide whether this is a home, an investment, or both, and judge it accordingly
Compare buying with renting and with REITs or funds for the same money
Budget the full cost, including stamp duty, registration, brokerage, GST and move-in costs
Calculate net yield and the appreciation needed to beat your alternatives
Keep EMIs within comfort and an emergency fund untouched
Verify RERA registration, developer track record and complaint history
Have an independent lawyer check title, encumbrances and approvals
Register at the real price and pay only through banking channels
Check how this purchase changes your real estate share of net worth
Walk away from any pitch built on urgency, cash or guaranteed returns

points: Most property losses come from predictable, avoidable mistakes rather than bad luck.
Budget the full cost of buying, and compare net yields and CAGRs, not headlines and stories.
Borrow only what you can carry through rate rises and income shocks, and only when the numbers support leverage.
Protect yourself legally: RERA checks, an independent lawyer, original documents and registration at the real price.
Avoid urgency-driven, cash-based or guaranteed-return pitches, and weak developers with risky payment plans.
Keep liquidity and diversification in mind, and remember that REITs, funds and other routes can often do the job better than another flat.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or tax advice. Examples are illustrative, and rules, rates and market conditions change. Consult a qualified property lawyer, a tax professional and a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making any property or investment decision.
